---
title: "Evaluation"
description: "Measure what a control does: automatic pre/post comparison from versions, and criteria-triggered impact measurement"
---

Once a [control](/guide/build/world-model/controls) states when to act and
what to do, **evaluation** answers the question that naturally follows, which
is whether it worked.

Evaluation lives at the control layer because the control already supplies
both halves of the measurement problem. Its **versions** define the unit of
comparison, recording which algorithm ran and when it changed, while its
**criteria** define the moment of measurement, since the same condition that
fires the action is the condition whose cost you want to know.

## Versioned controls

Each version of a control is a criteria and action pair. Exactly one version
is active at a time, and the platform records whenever the active version
switches:

```yaml
# replenishment.control.yml
control: replenishment
objective: "Never let a SKU run out"
owner: ops
for_each: sku_store
schedule: daily

versions:
  - name: reorder_at_zero
    criteria:
      type: trigger
      when: "{{inventory.on_hand}} == 0"
    action:
      order: "{{sales.daily_demand}} * 14"
      via: replenishment_reorder

  - name: forecast_depletion
    active: true
    criteria:
      type: trigger
      when: "{{inventory.on_hand}} < {{sales.daily_demand}} * {{skus.lead_time_days}}"
    action:
      order: "{{sales.daily_demand}} * 14"
      via: replenishment_reorder
```

Versioning is what makes a control evaluable in the first place. Answering
"did the change work?" requires a before and an after, or two algorithms to
compare, and the version history provides both without anyone having to
reconstruct what was running at a given time.

## Version comparison

When the active version switches, the pre/post comparison derives
automatically from the control itself, comparing the measures its criteria
read, along with the KPIs downstream of them in the
[Metric Tree](/guide/build/world-model/metric-tree), across the switch date.
Two versions can also run side by side, with some entities assigned to each,
which controls for seasonality and external shocks in a way that a simple
pre/post comparison cannot. In either case the comparison metric comes from
the control definition rather than from an analysis someone assembles by
hand, so every control accumulates a track record of what its changes did.

## Mechanistic impact measurement

Whereas version comparison observes how KPIs move, the longer-term method
prices the events themselves. The insight is that the criteria already mark
the moment that matters: if a control's criteria fire on a stockout, then
measurement should fire on that stockout too. The control simply declares
what each firing costs:

```yaml
evaluation:
  counterfactual_measure: sales.revenue   # what is lost while the criteria hold
  window: until_replenished               # from firing until the order lands
```

Each firing is then priced as the revenue lost at the SKU-store grain over
the window during which the condition held. A version's impact becomes the
sum of its priced events, so comparing versions turns into comparing priced
events rather than hoping that a KPI shift can be attributed to the change.
The counterfactual measure and its window resolve in the semantic engine,
which is where this mechanism will be built.

## Backtesting

A version does not need to run in production before it can be evaluated.
Executing its criteria against history produces a trace of every day it
would have fired, shown side by side with what the active version actually
did, and the same `evaluation` block prices that trace. You can therefore
backtest a proposed version before adopting it and measure it afterward, with
both answers coming from the same definitions.

## Learning drivers

Evaluation is also how the World Model learns causal magnitudes. The
[metric tree's](/guide/build/world-model/metric-tree) driver edges are
qualitative by design, stating what drives what but deliberately not how
much, because a magnitude can only be identified through intervention and a
control is the thing that intervenes. When a control acts on a driver, its
measured results (version comparisons, side-by-side runs, and priced firings)
estimate how much that driver moves the KPI. The estimate keeps updating as
the control continues to act, carries a confidence that grows with the
number of interventions, and supersedes any observational fit.

In other words, while the physics knows what drives what, a control learns
how much by acting. A KPI whose drivers carry no control-learned magnitudes
is being navigated on correlation alone, and the World Model graph makes this
visible by showing, for each edge, whether its magnitude comes from
interventions or from observation.

## Feeding the physics

Evaluation results flow back into
[calibration](/guide/build/world-model/calibration). When a change's measured
impact disagrees with what the model implied, the gap points at a specific
physical claim, such as a lead time or a demand response, and the physics
layer updates accordingly, so that the model the next decision runs on is
sharper than the one before it.
